chunks: PCB vs breadboard vs perfboard vs wiring vs IC.
The question: What are the tradeoffs of PCBs vs solderless breadboards vs soldered breadboards vs just soldering everything together with wires vs ICs?
A breadboard, a perfboard, point-to-point wiring, a PCB and an IC are different ways to build the same circuit, and each suits a different stage of a project.
A breadboard is fastest to change but has flaky contacts and extra stray capacitance and inductance. Perfboard and point-to-point are permanent but slow and hard to repeat.
A PCB is repeatable and compact. An IC costs the most to start but is cheapest per unit at huge volume.
Think of designing a house. A pencil sketch is quick to change but is not a house (the breadboard). A cardboard model is sturdier but each one is hand-made (perfboard).
A printed blueprint lets any builder make an identical house (the PCB). Building a factory that stamps out whole houses (the IC) only pays off if you sell enough of them.
The analogy leaves out electrical behavior: each step also changes how fast and how cleanly the circuit can run.
The decision is driven by what you need next.
A PCB is the default for anything that will be built more than a handful of times; a custom IC is justified only by volume or performance that discrete parts cannot reach.
Solderless breadboard: a plastic board with spring clips, so parts push in and need no solder.
Perfboard / point-to-point: soldered builds with a hole grid, or with parts wired directly together. Parasitic: unintended resistance, inductance or capacitance from the build.
NRE (non-recurring engineering): the one-time cost of design and tooling. Break-even volume: the number of units at which a higher-NRE, lower-unit-cost option becomes cheaper.
On a breadboard, a 100 mm jumper adds about 100 nanohenries of inductance, and the rows add about 10 picofarads.
Together they resonate near 1 over (2 pi square root of 10 to the -7 times 10 to the -11 ) equals 159 megahertz, so fast edges ring.
For cost, suppose a PCB has 150 USD of setup and 5 USD per unit, and hand wiring costs 25 USD per unit with no setup.
They match when 5 plus 150 over n equals 25 , so at n equals 7. 5 units. Above about eight units, the PCB wins. That is the whole idea.
"A breadboard is fastest to change but has flaky contacts and a few picofarads and nanohenries of parasitics, so it's for exploration at low frequency.
Perfboard or point-to-point is permanent but slow and not repeatable. A PCB takes days to fab but is repeatable, compact, with controlled impedance and cheap at volume.
An IC has the biggest up-front cost but the best size, power and performance at high volume. So you progress from breadboard to PCB, and to an IC only when volume justifies it."
